CALIFORNIA REGIONAL WATER QUALITY CONTROL BOARD
                         LAHONTAN REGION

                     MEETING OF OCTOBER 1, 2026
                        SOUTH LAKE TAHOE

ITEM 6
REVISED WASTE DISCHARGE REQUIREMENTS – TAHOE-TRUCKEE
SANITATION AGENCY WATER RECLAMATION PLANT



CHRONOLOGY
April 25, 1974       The Water Board adopted waste discharge requirements
                     (WDRs), Board Order No. 6-74-44 for the Tahoe-Truckee
                     Sanitation Agency (T-TSA) Water Reclamation Plant
                     (Facility). The beginning of the regulated history for this
                     facility.

May 12, 1977         The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-77-27 for the Facility.

July 9, 1981         The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-81-61 for the Facility.

September 17, 1981   The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-81-71 for the Facility.

February 19, 1987    The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-87-21 for the Facility.

April 11, 1990       The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-90-27 for the Facility.

October 3, 1996      The Water Board amended WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. 6-90-27A1 for the Facility.

May 9, 2002          The Water Board updated WDRs by adopting Board Order
                     No. R6T-2002-0030 for the Facility, the most recent
                     revisions to the WDRs




                                                                               6-1

BACKGROUND
The Facility is located approximately 3 miles east of the Town of Truckee. It is near
the southeastern bank of the Truckee River, with Martis Creek approximately a half
mile to the east.
The Facility serves the Town of Truckee and several surrounding communities,
including the North Tahoe Public Utility District, Tahoe City Public Utility District,
Olympic Valley Public Service District, Alpine Springs County Water District, and
Northstar Community Services District. The Facility is capable of transporting, treating
and disposing of a maximum 7-day average municipal wastewater flow, during the
summer months of 9.6 MGD.
The current WDRs for T-TSA were adopted in 2002. Since then, the Facility has
undergone operational improvements and conducted a fate and transport study
related to nutrient removal and groundwater quality. The operational changes and the
study have informed many of the revisions to the WDRs.



ISSUES
Should the Water Board adopt revised waste discharge requirements for the Truckee-
Tahoe Water Reclamation Plant to reflect changes in discharge conditions, update
monitoring and reporting requirements, and incorporate provisions consistent with
current regulatory standards and policies?



DISCUSSION
The proposed T-TSA WDRs reflects operational changes and updates certain
monitoring and reporting program (MRP) requirements. T-TSA requested that Water
Board staff review the existing WDRs from 2002 and consider revising it. There is
also a need to update the MRP to capture emerging constituents of concern and to
modernize analytical methods for other constituents that may otherwise be outdated.
Major revisions between the 2002 WDRs and the proposed WDRs include, but are
not limited to, the following:
   a. Findings have been updated to reflect conclusions from the 2024 fate and
      transport study and updated 303(d) list impaired water bodies.
   b. An effluent limitation for total nitrogen has been added.
   c. A biochemical oxygen demand effluent limitation has been added in place of a
      previously existing chemical oxygen demand limitation.
   d. Requirements have been added related to construction and new projects. This
      includes various stormwater pollution prevention controls as well as
      implementation of best management practices.




                                                                                    6-2

DISCUSSION
   e. Monitoring for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) has been added to
      the influent, effluent, and the main compliance groundwater well (Well 31) on a
      quarterly basis. Monitoring for PFAS has been added to upstream and
      downstream surface water stations in both Martis Creek and the Truckee River
      on an annual basis.
   f. Monitoring requirements have been updated to modernize
      constituents/methods, e.g., volatile organic compounds has replaced
      purgeable halocarbons/aromatics.
   g. Certain editorial changes to address typos and formatting issues.



SUSTAINABLE GROUNDWATER MANAGEMENT ACT BASINS
For purposes of the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, the California
Department of Water Resources identifies the following groundwater basin in Nevada
County, along with priority, near the discharge location within the Lahontan Region.

      Priority             Groundwater Basin
      Very Low             Martis Valley (6-067)

Source: Sustainable Groundwater Management Act Basin Prioritization



CLIMATE CHANGE RESPONSE
The revised waste discharge requirements for the Facility are consistent with
Resolution R6T-2019-0277, the Water Board’s Climate Change Mitigation and
Adaptation Strategy in the following key resources areas: (1) Protection of Wetlands,
Floodplains, and Headwaters; (2) Infrastructure Protection; and (3) Protection of
Groundwater Quality and Supply.
In particular, the revised waste discharge requirements establish updated effluent,
surface water, and groundwater limitations, enhance monitoring and reporting
requirements, and add to other permit provisions that help protect groundwater
quality, surface water quality, and sensitive habitats. These requirements are
consistent with the key resource areas identified in the Resolution, including the
protection of floodplains, and groundwater quality and supply.




                                                                                      6-3

BACKGROUND
Water Board staff has been providing annual updates regarding the Water Board’s
Enforcement Program for more than ten years. This agenda item will focus on
improvements and accomplishments since the 2025 Annual Enforcement Program
Update.

DISCUSSION
This agenda item will provide a presentation to the Water Board that includes the
following topics:
  •   Summary of fiscal year 2025/2026 violations and informal and formal
      enforcement actions to address those violations including comparison to prior
      fiscal years.
  •   Summary of Enforcement Program accomplishments in fiscal year 2025/2026.
  •   Summary of planned Enforcement Program improvements for fiscal year
      2026/2027.
  •   Summary of Enforcement Program priorities for fiscal year 2026/2027.
The enforcement priorities are as follows:
  •   Continue tracking and obtaining regulatory compliance within the various programs
      in the Region. Regulatory and permitting staff guide dischargers to compliance
      through reviewing monitoring reports, conducting inspections, cataloguing
      compliance violations, and issuing enforcement actions. Each of these activities
      form the basis for tracking and obtaining compliance with existing permits and
      ensuring water quality protection.
  •   Emphasize enforcement in areas that impact public drinking water supply in
      disadvantaged or severely disadvantaged communities, and in areas that directly
      impact Tribes or where there are long-standing environmental justice issues.
  •   Enforcement against alleged violations that are adversely affecting groundwater or
      surface water quality and beneficial uses. Examples may include unauthorized
      discharges of sewage, site cleanup and groundwater contamination sites,
      hazardous waste, and dredge/fill materials to creeks, springs, rivers, lakes, and
      wetlands.
  •   Improve Communication and Coordination with internal and external parties. Such
      external parties may include, but not limited to, municipal jurisdictions, state, and
      federal agencies. Continue coordination with existing external partners to identify
      Supplemental Environmental Projects (SEPs) opportunities as well as focus efforts
      on identifying new external partners to expand the available SEPs throughout the
      region. Additionally, provide meaningful public participation opportunities to
      disadvantaged communities and tribes in enforcement matters, improve data
      collection and availability of violation and enforcement information to minority and
      low-income communities, and ensure that effective cross-media coordination and
      accountability in addressing environmental justice issues.
This agenda item will also include a presentation from State Water Resource Control
Board’s Office of Enforcement regarding an overview of their role in assisting the
Lahontan region with enforcement actions.

                                                                                    7-2

 None

RECOMMENDATION
 This is an informational item only. No Water Board action is required for this item;
 however, the Water Board may provide direction to staff.
